content.thinking:
I'm piecing together the postmortem timeline: all 240 shopper monthly totals are off, starting with a purchase right after a deploy at 13:40 on Oct 17, and the evidence points to record_purchase no longer updating total_this_month_cents at the current running revision.

Now I'm drafting the symptom description for the report—settling on something like "Shopper monthly spend totals fell behind the purchases recorded against them" as the clearest framing of what the alert and account page actually showed users, then starting to lay out the causal chain beginning with the reconciliation failure itself.

Tracing the mechanism: purchases after the break were recorded without updating the stored monthly total, since record_purchase only advances total_cents without touching total_this_month_cents. I'm pinning this to revision 26f1d7e, which removed that update on the assumption the monthly figure would be derived on demand, and confirming it was running across all replicas by the relevant time. I'm also checking whether the earlier deploy can be ruled out — since there's no metrics window between it and onset, I instead lean on the alert timestamp, which dates the oldest affected purchase just after the revision's deploy time, effectively ruling out the earlier change as the cause.

The stored account total feeds spend_summary and spend_reconciliation, but nothing derives it on demand—S1's docstring confirms the account only carries running totals, so the premise that figures get "added up from history" never actually held. Citing F1 and S1 for this.

I need to be careful not to let the root cause depend on knowledge of how readers use the stored figure, since that rests on F1 — the mechanism itself should rest only on S1 and D1, with the reconciliation discrepancy (AL1) as what triggers the alert. I'll phrase it so root cause stays anchored to record_purchase no longer updating the stored total, without pulling in the reader-usage claim.

I note that doesn't fully negate the root cause since it's a separate matter from F1. Dating rule: changes get dated by their own commit's timestamp, and state gets evaluated as of that point.

For contributing factors, I'm flagging that no test caught the stored monthly total drifting out of sync with purchases when the write path change landed — a reconciliation test after recording would have failed before deploy. This is only partially addressed by the proposed fix's new tests, which cover the flagged code path but leave gaps.

I'm also proposing a process safeguard: before removing a stored field's writer, require review to check its readers. Then CF-2 covers detection — the spend-integrity check only runs periodically, so the fault went undetected for a stretch.

For CF-3, I'm noting that no one was paged when the alert fired, so rollback was left to no one in particular — I'll propose linking the alert to on-call paging. And CF-4 points out the same fault exists in main behind a feature flag.

For CF-4, I'm checking whether this still-at-risk flag counts as a contributing factor to this incident — it doesn't, since it wasn't the cause here. I also look at the deploy pipeline for signs of a reconciliation gate or canary rollout, but there's no evidence of staged deployment, so I can't claim that as a factor and should skip it. Then I start reviewing whether the repair script from F1 needs its own action item beyond the existing merge fix.

The rollback alone won't fix accounts whose totals are already wrong, so I'm proposing a mitigation step: run the repair script (dry run, then apply) to correct the drifted monthly totals, noting the timing caveat doesn't matter since we're still within the same month. For detection, I'm considering recommending the spend-integrity check run more frequently, though without a specific cadence yet.

Argus tied the deploy to the alert quickly and flagged a draft PR from Code-Fix, but declined to act since it couldn't verify the fix, recommending rollback instead. For what went wrong, I'm wary of vague claims like unread logs — the real gap seems to be that nobody got paged when the alert first fired.

For got lucky, I'm leaning toward the fact that the onset (Oct 17) and the alert (Oct 24) both fell within October, so the repair script's reliance on the current month still correctly rebuilt that month's figure — had the alert come after month-end, that repair path wouldn't have worked.

For still at risk, every purchase recorded while the buggy commit runs continues to leave stored monthly totals short, and totals already wrong stay wrong until repaired — the same flaw applies to the derive-the-month path too. I want to keep assumptions explicit: customer impact assessment rests on unmeasured reads of spend_summary, and I'm assuming all affected accounts' shortfall traces to this one change. I also need to avoid stating numeric figures while still allowing labels like the commit hash or PR identifier.

I'm settling on the symptom phrasing: shoppers' stored spend-this-month totals fell short of their recorded purchases — concise, active, and matching step one. This reaches a valid root cause, and I'm double-checking the phrasing contains no literal numbers.

action_items.item: After rolling back or deploying the fix, run scripts/repair_monthly_totals.py from draft pull request #334: export the accounts, run a dry run first, then apply and write the corrected totals back. A rollback alone keeps adding to totals that are already short.
Run the spend-integrity reconciliation much more often than its current schedule, so totals that drift from their purchases are flagged soon after a deploy.
Link the SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile alert to on-call paging so a person is paged when it fires.
Add a review rule: a change that stops writing a stored field must first move every reader of that field off it, and the reviewer checks this against the code that reads it.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' stored spend-this-month totals fell short of their recorded purchases: {A1} of {A2} shopper totals did not reconcile, the widest was short by {A3}, and the oldest affected purchase was recorded at {A4}.

Purchases recorded since then were written without moving the stored monthly total. At the running revision, record_purchase appends the purchase and adds to total_cents only, and leaves total_this_month_cents where it was.

ruled_out.what: The earlier deploy of revision 4c810f2 at {P1.1}: the alert dates the oldest affected purchase at {A4}, after the later deploy of 26f1d7e at {P2.1}.
A flag change, for example switching on the derive_the_month write path: the flag provider showed {T14.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus in the {T14.3} hour before {T14.4}.

causal_chain.step: The change behind this is the deploy of revision 26f1d7e at {P2.1}. Its diff removes the conditional addition to total_this_month_cents from record_purchase, on the premise that the month's figure adds up from the purchase history whenever it is needed. As of {T11.1}, all {T11.2} replicas were running that revision.

The change's premise did not hold, because the shop still keeps and uses the stored figure instead of working the month out from the purchases. The module that ran describes the account as carrying two running totals, kept on purpose instead of figures derived on demand, and says nothing in it notices when one copy moves without the other. According to Code-Fix's reading of the files that ran, spend_summary's average_spend_per_item_this_month divides the stored total_this_month_cents, and spend_reconciliation compares the stored figure against the purchases. That comparison is the check that fired.

input.cause_in_plain_words: A software change stopped the shop updating each shopper's saved "spent this month" figure when they bought something, but the shop still kept that figure, so it fell further behind their real purchases with every sale.

contributing_factors.factor: No test or review check was seen that would confirm recording a purchase leaves the stored monthly total in line with the purchases. The change removed the code that kept the total up to date while the stored figure was still kept and compared.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A test asserting that reconciliation finds no disagreement after a purchase is recorded would have failed on revision 26f1d7e before it was deployed.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The only thing seen to find this fault is the spend-integrity check, which runs every {A5} days. Requests kept succeeding and no metric moved, so nothing else caught the wrong totals.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A reconciliation that ran more often would have flagged the short totals soon after the deploy, before a week of purchases had been written short.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile was not linked to on-call paging, so no person was paged when it fired, even though the rollback is left for a person to do.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A paged on-call engineer could have acted on the recommended rollback as soon as the alert fired, which would have stopped more totals being written short.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

got_lucky: The month had not turned between the onset and the alert. The proposed repair script rebuilds totals from each purchase's current in-month marker, so it can still rebuild this month's correct figure; after the month turned it could not rebuild the affected month's totals.
went_well: Argus formed candidate causes naming the deploy of revision 26f1d7e within {T12.1 - alert_raised} of the alert, with the onset placed at the first affected purchase.
Argus did not roll back itself, because nothing would show whether the rollback worked within the time it waits; it recommended the rollback for a person instead.
Code-Fix opened draft pull request #334, with a fix, tests and a repair script, within {T19.1 - alert_raised} of the alert.

input.root_cause: Revision 26f1d7e changed record_purchase so that it appends the purchase and adds to total_cents, but no longer adds the price to total_this_month_cents. The account still stores total_this_month_cents as its own copy of the month's spending, and nothing on this write path brings it back in line with the purchases, so every current-month sale recorded since then left that stored total short by the price of the sale.
input.still_at_risk: While revision 26f1d7e runs, every current-month purchase keeps leaving shoppers' saved monthly totals short, and totals that are already short stay wrong until they are repaired; the write path behind the derive_the_month choice in the code that ran also leaves the month total unchanged in the same way.
input.symptom: Shoppers' stored spend-this-month totals fell short of the purchases recorded against them
